title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed.), 5.8 Evaluating point forecast accuracy
publisher: Rob J Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos (OTexts)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. MAE and RMSE are scale-dependent and cannot compare series in different units; MAPE is undefined at zero and unstable near zero; MASE scales errors by a naive or seasonal naive forecast so series can be compared, and below 1 beats naive; points to section 5.4 where non-zero mean residuals indicate bias.

title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed.), 6.7 Judgmental adjustments
publisher: Rob J Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos (OTexts)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Adjust only for important information not in the model (promotions, events); use sparingly; document and justify; larger adjustments tend to be more accurate than small ones; small upward adjustments can add optimism; adjusting to chase patterns is ineffective.

title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed.), Chapter 11 Forecasting hierarchical and grouped time series
publisher: Rob J Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos (OTexts)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Series split by product or place form hierarchies; forecasts should be coherent so parts add up to totals; bottom-up, top-down, middle-out and reconciliation approaches.

title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed.), 13.2 Time series of counts
publisher: Rob J Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos (OTexts)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Croston's method (1972) for intermittent demand smooths non-zero demand sizes and inter-arrival times separately and forecasts their ratio; it is biased and has no algebraic prediction intervals but is widely used; continuous methods are fine for large counts, small counts need care.

title: Safety stock
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Encyclopedia summary of the textbook formulas, citing Hopp and Spearman (Factory Physics), Nahmias and Ballou: SS = z x sqrt(E(L) x var(D) + E(D)^2 x var(L)); demand-only form z x sigma(D) x sqrt(L); ROP = E(L) x E(D) + SS; z about 1.65 for 95%; Type I (cycle) and Type II (fill rate) service. Used for the standard formula only, credited to the textbooks.

title: NORM.S.INV function
supports: Opened with WebFetch. NORM.S.INV(probability) returns the inverse of the standard normal cumulative distribution; #NUM! if probability is 0 or less, or 1 or more.

title: Economic order quantity
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Encyclopedia summary: Ford W. Harris (1913, 'How many parts to make at once'); Q* = sqrt(2DK/h); assumes constant demand and a fixed cost per order; Q* does not depend on unit price; quantity discounts as an extension.

title: Newsvendor model
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Encyclopedia summary: critical fractile q* = F^-1((p - c)/p) with underage cost p - c and overage cost c when leftovers have no value; single period, perishable goods; Edgeworth (1888) and Arrow, Harris and Marschak (1951).

title: The Bullwhip Effect in Supply Chains
publisher: MIT Sloan Management Review (Hau L. Lee, V. Padmanabhan, Seungjin Whang)
supports: Opened with WebFetch (introduction only; rest is paywalled). Spring 1997. P&G Pampers and HP printer examples of order swings growing upstream; consequences: excess inventory, weaker service, lost sales, misguided capacity plans, poor transport, missed production schedules.

title: Bullwhip effect
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Encyclopedia summary of Lee, Padmanabhan and Whang (1997), Management Science 43(4): four causes (demand forecast updating, order batching, price fluctuations, rationing and shortage gaming) and countermeasures (information sharing, smoother and smaller orders, everyday low pricing, allocation on past sales). Used because the primary paper is paywalled.

title: Toyota Production System
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Two pillars, jidoka and just-in-time; each process replenishes what the next one takes; roles of Sakichi Toyoda, Kiichiro Toyoda and Taiichi Ohno.

title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.2.1 What is acceptance sampling?
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Acceptance sampling accepts or rejects a lot from a random sample; used when testing is destructive or full inspection costly or slow; judges lots rather than estimating quality; not a substitute for process control; Dodge and Romig.

title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.1 What are control charts?
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Control charts plot a measure over time with a centre line and limits usually at three standard deviations; a point outside signals a need to look for an assignable cause.
